query: How do opportunistic scanners locate an EC2-hosted API endpoint that was never published anywhere?

I stood up an API server on EC2 for a mobile app that hasn't shipped yet, and the URL isn't linked from anywhere public, but I'm already seeing strangers probing random paths on it. How did they find it?
unknown IPs hitting unpublished server URL
If nobody knows my server address because I never shared it, how are random people still sending requests to made-up paths on it?
Strangers are trying to open pages on my company's server even though we never told anyone its address, and I don't understand how they even know it exists.
Is deleted data on a solid-state drive recoverable if it was never overwritten?

We handle sensitive data on machines with SSDs instead of spinning disks, and I need to know whether deleting files is actually enough before the hardware leaves our control. Can anything still be pulled off the drive afterward?
can deleted SSD data be recovered

I know that on a regular hard drive deleted files are still sitting there until something writes over them, but I'm not sure if the same thing is true for an SSD. Can someone still get those files back?
If I delete private files from a laptop with one of the newer drives that has no moving parts, can someone still dig them back up?
Does possessing both the plaintext and the ransomware-encrypted version of millions of files help recover the encryption key?

Our file server got encrypted by ransomware but we have clean backups of nearly every one of those files. Could lining up the originals against the encrypted copies help us work out the key instead of paying?
recover ransomware key using unencrypted backups

I thought that if you have the before and after version of a file you can sort of reverse engineer the scrambling. Would having thousands of matching pairs make it realistic to figure out a ransomware key?
All our company files got locked by a virus, but we still have copies of the originals. Can someone use the originals to unlock the locked ones?
Does salting meaningfully slow an offline dictionary attack once the attacker already has the hash file?

I'm reviewing how we store credentials and I always assumed adding a random value per user was the main defense. If someone dumps our database they get that value too, so does it actually buy us anything?
does salting stop password cracking after breach

I learned that salting stops precomputed hash tables because you'd need too much storage, but I'm confused about why people say it wouldn't have helped in big password leaks. Is it useless once the attacker steals the file?
After a big website leak everyone said the passwords should have had extra random characters mixed in. Would that really have stopped them from being figured out?
Are the human-manipulation techniques documented two decades ago still a realistic attack vector against modern organizations?

We've got strong access controls, encryption and identity checks across our systems, so I'm trying to judge how much effort to put into training staff against people who just talk their way in. Is that still a serious risk?
is social engineering still a real threat
I just read an old book about tricking people into handing over information, but that was a long time ago. With how easy it is to verify things now, are those tricks still working on companies?
Do people really still get fooled into giving away passwords or private company details just by someone asking them nicely over the phone?
Can a client be fingerprinted on a wireless network when its hardware address is forged and rotated?

I run the guest wireless for a small shop and a few machines keep joining with obviously fake hardware addresses that change every time I block one. Is there anything else I can use to pin down which device it is?
identify device spoofed MAC address wifi
I thought every network card has one permanent address you can block, but these users seem to just make up a new one each time. Is there some other way to tell the same laptop is coming back?

Someone keeps using my shop's free internet to do something my provider warned me about, and every time I block them they come straight back under a different name. How do I find out who it actually is?
How can a chat service defend against clients tampering with outbound packets to evade server-side moderation and rate limits?

I operate a chat room on an abandoned Java/Flash platform where some users run a packet editing tool to dodge mutes and the message rate limit. IP bans don't help because they just switch addresses, so what can I actually do about it?
stop users editing packets bypass chat limits
Some people in my chat room use a program that changes the data their client sends before it reaches us, which lets them spam and ignore being muted. Can this be blocked from the server side?
A few people in my chat room use some tool that lets them flood messages and ignore being silenced, and banning them doesn't stick. Is there any way to stop them for good?
What controls have enterprises adopted to protect confidential data on devices subject to warrantless border inspection, and what do those controls cost?

I support a team that travels internationally with company laptops that can be inspected and copied at the border without a warrant. What approaches do IT departments actually use to keep that data out of reach, and how expensive are they?
protecting corporate data laptop border search

I read that officials can take and copy a traveler's laptop at the border without needing a warrant. What do companies do about that for employees carrying confidential work, and does it cost them much?
My work laptop could be taken and copied when I fly into the country, and I'm worried about the private company files on it. What do businesses normally do to prepare for that?
What evidentiary value does a handwritten signature retain given how easily it can be forged or repudiated, and why has digital signing not displaced it?
We're deciding whether to keep collecting ink signatures on contracts or move to cryptographic signing. Does a handwritten one actually prove anything, and why hasn't the digital option taken over?
why handwritten signatures still used digital signatures
My own signature looks different every time I write it, so I don't see how it proves I signed something or stops someone copying it. Why are we still using them instead of the cryptographic kind?
Anyone could copy the way I sign my name, and I could just say a signature on a contract wasn't mine. So why do we still sign things by hand?
What attacks become possible when an adversary can arbitrarily set the system clock on a host, and have any been observed in practice?

I set my machine's date far into the future for testing and suddenly every site failed with a certificate date error that I couldn't click past. How much of a system's security actually depends on the clock being right?
security risks of wrong system clock

When I moved my computer's date forward by a couple of centuries, websites stopped loading and complained that my clock was ahead. I'm curious what an attacker could pull off if they could change the time themselves.
I changed the date on my computer to a year far in the future and now no websites will open at all, which makes me wonder what someone could do if they messed with my clock on purpose.
If JWTs are validated without a server-side lookup, how can a revocation endpoint actually invalidate an already-issued token?

My app uses self-contained tokens that aren't stored server side, and I'm wiring up a Sign Out button that calls the revocation endpoint. What stops the client from continuing to use the token it already has?
revoke stateless JWT without database
I thought the whole point of these tokens is that the server doesn't keep a copy so it skips a lookup, but you're also supposed to be able to revoke them. How can both be true at the same time?
When I press sign out on a site, I expect to have to log in again, but I was told the site doesn't actually keep track of my login. How does signing out work then?
What hardening steps prevent network-attached printers from being reached and driven by remote attackers?
After reading about tens of thousands of printers being made to print attacker-supplied messages, I want to lock down the printers and similar devices on our network. Where should I start?
how to secure network printer from attacks
I heard someone took over a huge number of printers remotely and made them print whatever they wanted. I don't know much about networking, so what would I actually change to keep mine safe?
I read that strangers made thousands of printers spit out messages they didn't ask for, and now I'm worried about mine. What should I do to stop that happening to me?
Is there still pedagogical value in teaching buffer overflow exploitation when the course has to disable DEP, stack canaries and ASLR to make it work?

I'm putting together secure coding training for my team and the memory corruption module only works with modern protections switched off. Is that still worth covering, or is it a historical curiosity now?
are buffer overflows still worth learning
In class we had to turn off a bunch of memory protections to get a stack smash to work, which felt artificial to me. If those defenses are on by default everywhere, why are we still studying this?
My students say this old style of attack can't happen on today's computers because the protections are built in. Is it still worth spending class time on it?
Can a VPS host read the memory or disk contents of a guest instance, and can a tenant provide assurance that it cannot?

I host my clients' data on rented virtual servers rather than hardware I own, and clients keep asking whether anyone at the hosting company could look at it. Is that technically possible for them, and what can I tell clients?
can VPS provider read customer data
I rent a virtual machine from a hosting company and I know they own the actual hardware underneath. Does that mean they could look at my files even if their terms don't say so?
I keep my customers' information on a server I rent from an online company, and I promised them nobody else sees it. Could the rental company itself look at it if they wanted to?
Is covert cloning of an access credential carried in a pocket feasible during a brief physical brush-past?
I'm assessing the access control on a facility where entry uses a card kept in people's pockets with no PIN. Could someone copy one of those cards just by walking into the holder for a second or two?
can access card be cloned through pocket
Someone with a bag knocked into my back pocket on the street, and the next day my card-locked unit was opened without any damage. Could a device in a bag copy a card that quickly through clothing?
A stranger bumped into my pocket where I keep my entry card, and the next day someone got into my storage unit without breaking anything. Could they have copied my card just by brushing past me?
What triggers a new-device sign-in notification from a provider when the same machine and public IP are used every time?

I sign in from the same laptop and the same egress IP every time, but the provider emails me a new-device alert on every login. What is it actually keying off, and could my browser privacy extensions be causing it?
new device sign in email every login same computer

I keep getting warnings that my account was accessed from a new machine even though it's always the same laptop. I use a VPN with one fixed address and some privacy add-ons, so could that be confusing it?
Every single time I log in on my own laptop I get an email saying someone signed in from a new device, and I can't tell if that means somebody is really getting into my account.
When is accepting an unmitigable threat and adjusting the business model a more defensible choice than investing in a control that cannot work?

I'm advising a client on a protection scheme where the content has to be exposed to the end user at some point, so any control can ultimately be worked around. At what point do I recommend they stop spending on defense and just absorb the loss?
when to accept a risk you cannot prevent

We talked in class about protections that can always be bypassed because the data has to be readable eventually. Is it ever the right answer to just not defend against something and deal with the consequences instead?
If there's no way to actually stop a certain kind of theft from happening to my business, is it reasonable to just accept it and change how I make money instead of paying for protection?
How credible is the claim that IPSec has been weakened by state-level actors, and can it be configured to remain trustworthy?

We run IPSec tunnels because they're fast and widely supported, but I keep seeing claims that intelligence agencies targeted the protocol. Should I move to a different VPN, or can I configure IPSec so it still holds up?
is IPSec broken by NSA credible
I read that leaked documents said a government agency went after IPSec, but I can't tell how much of that is hype. Is it actually unsafe, or does it depend on how you set it up?
People online say a government agency can read traffic protected by the VPN technology we use at work, and I can't tell if that's a real problem or just scare talk.
What is the realistic exposure from a USB device that impersonates a network adapter to hijack outbound requests and plant persistent cached iframes?

I'm trying to write guidance for staff about the gadget that plugs into a USB port, pretends to be a wired network connection and poisons the browser cache. Does locking the screen actually protect a machine, or do people need to shut down?
PoisonTap risk how worried should I be

I read about a small USB gadget that tricks a computer into treating it as a wired network and then plants bad content in the browser. Does this work on everyone, or only certain systems and browsers?
I read about a little device someone can plug into a laptop's USB port while you step away for a minute, and it apparently gets into your accounts. Is locking my screen enough to stop that?
Does the abrupt end-of-development notice on the TrueCrypt site reflect a genuine advisory, and should existing volumes be migrated?

We encrypt a number of volumes with TrueCrypt and its site now warns it may have unfixed problems and points everyone at the platform's built-in encryption. Is that notice legitimate, and do we need to move our data?
is TrueCrypt warning real should I stop using it

The TrueCrypt site suddenly says it isn't secure and tells people to switch to the encryption built into their operating system, which seems odd. Is that an actual announcement or did someone take over the page?
The website for the program I use to lock my files now says it isn't safe and that I should move everything somewhere else, and I don't know whether to believe it.
Can software patches address the Spectre class of attacks generally, or only the specific exploit variants already published?

I'm reading the Spectre paper to decide how to prioritize patching our fleet, and the authors say known exploits can be blocked in software but the underlying issue is hard to mitigate. Does that mean new variants will keep slipping past the patches?
how serious is Spectre really
I read that the harder of the two recent processor flaws can only have its known attacks patched, which sounds like future ones won't be covered. Is that actually how bad it is?
I keep seeing alarming headlines about a flaw in computer chips that updates apparently can't fully fix. Should I actually be worried about this?
Can an attacker append crafted bytes to a tampered binary so that it still produces the original MD5 digest?
We publish an MD5 digest alongside our installer so users can verify the download. Could someone insert malicious code and then pad the file until the digest matches the one we published?
forge file to match original MD5 hash
If you add bad code to a program the checksum obviously changes, but could you keep tacking on extra junk bytes and trying combinations until you land back on the original value?
Download pages give you a code to check that the file wasn't altered, but could someone sneak something harmful into the file and still make that code come out the same?
How should an unauthorized finder disclose credentials and access they discovered on an institution's network without exposing themselves to disciplinary or legal consequences?

While poking around machines I only have user access to, I found an administrator password sitting in plaintext in a leftover setup file, and it turns out it opens up far more than I expected. Should I report this, and how do I do it without getting myself in trouble?
report security hole found at school without punishment

I'm a student who was experimenting on the school computers and ended up finding an admin password left behind in a config file that gives access to staff files and the servers. I want to tell someone before a bad actor finds it, but I'm scared I'll be blamed.
I accidentally came across a password on my school's computers that lets anyone get into teachers' files and change accounts, and I want to warn them without getting into trouble myself.
How can a third-party site display a visitor's social network profile name without the visitor having granted that site any permission?

I'm looking at adding one of those chat widgets to our site and noticed that on another site it greeted me by my real name from a social network I never connected to it. How does that widget get the visitor's identity?
website knows my Facebook name chat widget
A site I'd never visited before popped up a chat box with my actual name on it, tied to a social network account. I never approved any sharing, so how does the site get that?
A website I just opened showed a little chat box in the corner with my real name in it, and it creeps me out because I never gave that site anything.
Does including a server-generated token in a form actually block submissions originating from another origin, given the token is visible in the page source?

I need to make sure my form can only be submitted from my own site and I've been told checking the referrer isn't dependable, so I added a generated token field. Does that genuinely stop submissions from elsewhere when the token value is right there in the HTML?
does nonce prevent form submission from other domain

I only want my website's form to accept entries sent from my own site, and I added a hidden code to the page to try to enforce that. Does that actually work?
What threat does a SIM lock code actually mitigate, given a thief is likely to discard the card immediately?
I'm writing device security guidance for staff phones and I'm unsure whether to require the card-level lock code. A thief will just pull the card out anyway, so is it worth mandating?
is SIM PIN worth using

I get why you lock the phone itself, but the card lock seems pointless since a thief throws the card away right off, and it just stops an honest finder from contacting me. Is there actually a point to it?
My phone asks for a separate code for the little card inside whenever I restart it, and I'm wondering whether turning that off would put me at any risk.
What is the realistic interval between a card being captured at a compromised ATM and a fraudulent withdrawal using the cloned credential?

I'm looking at a disputed transaction where an unauthorized withdrawal happened about a minute after the legitimate cardholder used the same machine. Is that turnaround plausible for a card-capture device, or does it rule it out?
how fast can skimmed card be used

My understanding is that a device on a cash machine copies your card details and PIN, but I don't know how long it takes before the thief can actually pull money out. Could it happen within a minute of the original withdrawal?

My daughter took out cash and a stranger withdrew money from her account one minute later, and the bank insists that is impossible unless she handed over her card. Could someone have copied her card and used it that quickly?
What prevents an authenticated client from extracting its bearer token and replaying arbitrary requests to the API outside the official app?

My app logs in against a token endpoint and then sends that token on every call to the API. What stops a user from grabbing their own token and hammering the endpoints from a request tool to create masses of fake content, and does serving it over TLS cover this?
prevent API abuse with stolen bearer token from own app

I know the login returns a token that gets attached to later requests, but the user can see their own token. Couldn't they just use it outside the app to spam my service, or does encryption in transit handle that?
My app talks to a server to log people in and save their posts, and I'm worried someone could skip the app entirely and flood it with fake entries.
Does signing in to Windows with a vendor-linked account rather than a local one meaningfully change the threat model, including key escrow?

I set up my work machines with local accounts instead of linking them to the vendor's online account because it feels like extra exposure. Beyond the privacy angle, is the local option actually more secure, and does the vendor end up holding my encryption keys?
local account vs Microsoft account security
I use a local login on my Windows machine because tying it to an online account seems like one more way in for an attacker. Is it genuinely safer, or is that just a feeling?
I log into my computer with an account that only exists on the machine instead of the one tied to the company's website, and I want to know if that actually keeps my stuff safer.
What messaging architecture would prevent a seized admin device from exposing the full membership roster of a large activist group?

I help run large coordination groups on a messaging app where the organizer's handset can expose everyone else's identities if it gets unlocked. Would moving to a platform with sender anonymity features actually protect the membership, or do we need something built for anonymous participation?
protect group member identities if admin phone unlocked

I've read that the messaging app our group uses rolled its own encryption, but even setting that aside, one admin's unlocked phone revealed tens of thousands of members. What setup would stop a single person's device from giving everyone away?
I'm in a very large group chat and someone who runs it was pressured into unlocking their phone, which exposed everyone in the group. How can we chat without putting each other at risk like that?
What data extraction is feasible against a stolen Mac laptop during the window before a remote wipe reaches it?

My work Mac was taken from my car and nobody noticed for two days, and IT will only wipe it once it comes online. Assuming the thief actually wants the data rather than the hardware, how much of my saved browser credentials and notes could they get at?
stolen macbook can thief access my data

Someone stole my laptop two days ago and all my passwords were saved on it, and I'm scared they can open everything up before it gets erased.
What is the appropriate response to an inbound fax flood that consumes toner and paper on our fax lines?

black fax attack what to do
Someone sent our office a run of all-dark fax pages overnight, which I gather is a deliberate way to waste supplies. Is there anything we can actually do once it starts?
I came into work and every fax machine had spat out stacks of nearly black pages with a rude message on them, and I don't know who to call or how to make it stop.
What operational practices limit exposure when unlocking a password manager vault on a machine you do not control?

I travel a lot and often need credentials from my password manager on borrowed machines, either through the web interface or by installing the extension there. What residue does that leave on the host and how do I clean it up afterwards?
using password manager safely on someone else's computer

When I open my password vault on a borrowed laptop I end up copying and pasting passwords, and I think the extension also saves an encrypted copy of my data on that machine. What should I be doing to avoid leaving things behind?
I need to get a password out of my password app while using a friend's computer, and I'm worried about what stays on their machine afterwards.
Which TPM 2.0 operations actually require the owner authorization value, and how can a candidate owner password be verified read-only from Linux?

what is TPM owner password used for

My laptop's security chip apparently has an owner password that Windows set by itself, and I don't understand what it protects or how I'd check whether a password I have is the right one.
With a verifier-based protocol like SRP6a, how can a server enforce that a forced password change actually results in a different password?

force password change SRP verifier detect same password

Is wiped free space distinguishable from ordinary unallocated space during forensic examination, and does writing and deleting filler data conceal it?

I run secure-erase tooling over the free space on a drive before it changes hands. Can an examiner tell afterwards that an overwrite happened, and would filling part of the drive with throwaway files and deleting them hide that?
can forensics detect that free space was wiped

If I use a program that properly erases deleted files so they can't be brought back, can someone looking at the computer later tell that I did that?
What common characteristics of Adobe's file formats account for their disproportionate share of parser vulnerabilities?

why adobe file formats have so many vulnerabilities

The programs that open Adobe documents and animations seem to need security fixes constantly compared to other software, and I'm curious what it is about those file types.
Does a higher assurance level under ISO/IEC 15408 imply the evaluated product is more secure than one certified at a lower level?
I'm comparing two certified products for a procurement and one carries a higher assurance rating than the other. Can I treat the higher-rated one as the safer choice?
does higher EAL mean more secure

Two products we're looking at both have security certifications but one is at a higher numbered level, and I want to know if that just means it's the safer product.
What drove the sudden proliferation of cookie consent notices across sites in multiple jurisdictions?

why do all websites ask about cookies now

Every website I open makes me click a box about cookies before I can read anything, and I want to know why they all started doing that at the same time.

stack grows down but overflow overwrites return address

Is keystroke logging on employee endpoints an accepted control in regulated industries, or an outlier practice?

do companies really use keyloggers on employees

What property does a distributed ledger add to secure messaging that existing end-to-end encrypted protocols do not already provide?

why use blockchain for secure messaging

Can outbound network traffic originating from browser extensions be blocked at the browser or OS level without relying on another extension?

block firefox extensions from sending data out

verify PDF timestamp against timestamp authority record

share dhparam between virtual hosts

does resetting BIOS password trigger bitlocker recovery

prevent sftp user symlink outside chroot

sslstrip when user types https directly

sqlmap crawl skip prompts non interactive
